---
title: T3 - Running scenarios
jupyter: python3
---

A single run tells you very little, because cervical cancer is rare and every
run uses different random numbers. In this tutorial we run the same model five
times to see how much of the result is noise, then compare three vaccination
coverage levels with uncertainty bands around each one.

## How much of this is noise?

Give `ss.MultiSim` one sim and a number of runs, and it makes that many copies
with different random seeds:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
import hpvsim as hpv

PARS = dict(
    location       = 'nigeria',
    genotypes      = [16, 18, 'hi5', 'ohr'],
    n_agents       = 2000,
    start          = 1990,
    stop           = 2040,
    ms_agent_ratio = 25,
    verbose        = 0,
)

msim = ss.MultiSim(hpv.Sim(**PARS), n_runs=5)
msim.run(verbose=0)
fig = msim.plot('all_hpv_asr_cancer_incidence', lines=True)
```

Five lines, one model. The spread between them is the stochastic noise floor of
this configuration: any difference between two scenarios smaller than this
spread is not a result.

The individual runs are in `msim.sims`:

```{python}
for s in msim.sims:
    print(f'seed {s.pars.rand_seed}: {float(s.results.all_hpv.cum_cancers[-1]):>10,.0f} cancers')
```

## Reduce to a median and a band

Without `lines=True`, `msim.plot()` shows the median of the runs and a 95% interval:

```{python}
fig = msim.plot('all_hpv_asr_cancer_incidence')
```

The results across the runs are in `msim.results`, named as for one sim, with the runs as their first axis: `msim.results.all_hpv.cum_cancers` has one row per run. `median()` and `quantiles()` reduce them, and the individual runs are still in `msim.sims`:

```{python}
r = msim.results.all_hpv.cum_cancers
low, mid, high = r.quantiles([0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
print(f'Cancers by 2040: {float(mid[-1]):,.0f} '
      f'(10-90%: {float(low[-1]):,.0f} to {float(high[-1]):,.0f})')
```

Prefer `median()` over `mean()` for cancers, infections and prevalence. These
are not normally distributed across seeds, so a mean plus or minus two standard
deviations is not a 95% interval and its lower edge can fall below zero.

## Compare vaccination coverage levels

Write a function that builds the sim of one scenario, then hand them all to `ss.parallel` with the number of runs of each. Here we run three coverage levels with five seeds each, to 2060 so the vaccinated girls reach the ages where cervical cancer occurs:

```{python}
LONG = dict(PARS, stop=2060)
COVERAGES = [0.0, 0.5, 0.9]
N_SEEDS = 5

girls = ss.ppl.female & (ss.ppl.age >= 9) & (ss.ppl.age < 14)

def make_sim(coverage):
    """One sim for a given vaccination coverage."""
    vaccination = ss.vaccinate(hpv.vx('bivalent'), where=girls, coverage=coverage, start=2010)
    return hpv.Sim(**LONG, label=f'coverage={coverage:.0%}', interventions=vaccination)

sims = [make_sim(coverage=c) for c in COVERAGES]
msim = ss.parallel(*sims, n_runs=N_SEEDS, verbose=0)
```

Each result now has the runs of every scenario, and `quantiles()` reduces each scenario on its own, giving one row per scenario and quantile:

```{python}
years = np.asarray(msim.sims[0].results.timevec.years)
i2055 = int(np.argmin(abs(years - 2055)))

asr = msim.results.all_hpv.asr_cancer_incidence.quantiles([0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
asr = np.asarray(asr).reshape(len(COVERAGES), 3, -1) # Scenario, quantile, time
for i, cov in enumerate(COVERAGES):
    low, mid, high = asr[i, :, i2055]
    print(f'coverage={cov:>4.0%}  incidence in 2055: {mid:5.1f} '
          f'({low:.1f} to {high:.1f}) per 100,000')
```

Read the bands, not just the medians. Where two scenarios' bands sit clear of
each other, the difference between them is a result. Where they overlap, it is
not — at this population size and with five seeds those two scenarios are
indistinguishable, however different their medians look. Either report that as
the answer, or raise `n_agents` and `N_SEEDS` until the bands separate.

## One thing that will catch you out

Running many sims sends each one to a separate process, so the sims that come
back are copies, not the objects you put in. Always read results from
`msim.sims`, never from the list you passed to `ss.parallel`. Building a
MultiSim from sims you have already run yourself is the one case where the two
are the same objects.

A larger worked sweep, with 20 seeds of each scenario, is in `examples/m07_uq_sweep.py`.
